concepts.title: The Meaning of Freedom: Absence of External Interference

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Meaning of Freedom: Absence of External Interference' refers to.
questions.a: In its core sense freedom is the absence of externally imposed constraints: no outsider -- ruler, crowd or custom -- stands in the way of what a person could otherwise think, say or do. But constraint-free life is not lawless; rules that prevent one person from harming another protect rather than destroy freedom.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Meaning of Freedom: Absence of External Interference'.
questions.a: Freedom means no arbitrary external interference -- and only rules against harm shrink it.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Meaning of Freedom: Absence of External Interference' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: keps102.txt lines 1-90 (introduction and meaning of freedom, absence of external interference, constraints and their justification))

concepts.title: Freedom as the Development of One's Own Self

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Freedom as the Development of One's Own Self' refers to.
questions.a: Beyond being left alone, freedom is also positive: the growth of a person into a self-directing individual able to make and act on genuine choices. This view values education, self-discipline and openness of options -- a person shackled by ignorance or fear is unfree even if nobody is visibly forcing her.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Freedom as the Development of One's Own Self'.
questions.a: Real freedom is self-direction, not just an empty street -- capacities and options are part of liberty.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Freedom as the Development of One's Own Self' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: keps102.txt lines 90-170 (positive dimension of freedom, development of the individual, self-mastery and choice))

concepts.title: Why Freedom Matters: Moral Autonomy and Its Limits

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Why Freedom Matters: Moral Autonomy and Its Limits' refers to.
questions.a: Freedom matters because people are moral agents: they must decide for themselves what is good and bear responsibility for the choices they make. Choices that harm others are where society may intervene -- harm to self, however, is generally not enough to justify coercion, though debates continue at the margins.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Why Freedom Matters: Moral Autonomy and Its Limits'.
questions.a: Moral responsibility presupposes choice -- protect choice, and only police harm to others.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Why Freedom Matters: Moral Autonomy and Its Limits' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: keps102.txt lines 170-250 (why do we need freedom, moral basis, harm principle, limits of freedom))

concepts.title: Swaraj and Gandhi's View of Freedom

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Swaraj and Gandhi's View of Freedom' refers to.
questions.a: For Gandhi, swaraj meant more than throwing out foreign rulers: it demanded self-rule in the deepest sense -- discipline over one's own desires, courage rather than fear, and village-level self-reliance. Political freedom without this inner restraint would merely change masters.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Swaraj and Gandhi's View of Freedom'.
questions.a: Swaraj is rule over oneself first -- fearlessness and self-restraint are the raw material of real independence.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Swaraj and Gandhi's View of Freedom' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.4 (source: keps102.txt lines 250-340 (swaraj in the Indian freedom struggle, Gandhi's conception, critique of modernity, self-rule))

concepts.title: Freedom of Expression and Its Importance

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Freedom of Expression and Its Importance' refers to.
questions.a: Freedom of expression lets people speak, write, publish and disagree without fear, and it does double duty: it lets individuals develop their minds, and it keeps governments under the criticism they need. Reasonable limits -- defamation, incitement to violence -- protect other people's equal claims without silencing dissent.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Freedom of Expression and Its Importance'.
questions.a: Free speech builds both the self and the watchdog -- limits only where speech harms others.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Freedom of Expression and Its Importance' taught, and from which source text?
